content.p: On the afternoon of Tuesday 10 February 2026, an 18-year-old named Jesse Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother at their home in Tumbler Ridge, a mining town in northeastern British Columbia, then went to the local secondary school and killed five students and an educational assistant. She died at the school from what police described as a self-inflicted wound. Eight people were dead besides the shooter, and many others were injured or caught in a lockdown. It was the deadliest rampage in Canada since the Nova Scotia attacks of 2020, according to the Associated Press.

The shooter's death means there will be no trial of her. The months since have instead produced four separate efforts to answer how it happened: a long RCMP investigation into where the guns came from, a coroner's inquest ordered by the province, a growing set of lawsuits in California that accuse the company behind ChatGPT of failing to warn police, and, on 6 October 2026, a US criminal charge against a man accused of conspiring with her. He has been charged, not convicted.

The RCMP said it was told of an active shooter at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School at about 1:20 p.m. Pacific time. Officers from the local detachment arrived within two minutes, and the police said there was active gunfire and that rounds were fired toward officers as they approached. Police entered the building and within minutes found the shooter dead.

The killings at the home came first, Deputy Commissioner Dwayne McDonald told reporters. A young female relative who was at the house went to a neighbour, who called police, and officers did not reach the house until about 2.45 p.m., according to The Guardian's account of the briefing. The school is about 1.6 kilometres from the family home, Global News reported.

Inside the school, one victim was found in a stairwell and, McDonald believed, the rest in the library. The Associated Press quoted a mother, Shelley Quist, who said she thought Grade 7 and 8 students were upstairs in the library. Her 17-year-old son Darian, a Grade 12 student, told CBC that the lockdown began at around 1:30 p.m., that he and classmates barricaded the doors with tables and discussed escape routes, and that they waited about two and a half hours before RCMP officers escorted them out. He said he did not hear any of the shooting from where he was, since the school is spread out.

Police evacuated more than 100 students and staff to the community centre. Two people with serious injuries were flown to hospital, and about 25 others were assessed at the local medical centre; the RCMP said that after assessment no discernible physical injuries were identified in that group. CBC later reported 27 injured.

Police first reported ten dead including the shooter, according to Q107 Toronto, and the RCMP corrected that to nine, including the shooter, on 11 February: a woman it had thought dead had survived and was one of two seriously injured people flown to hospital, a 12-year-old and a 19-year-old, both in serious condition at that point. The final toll was eight victims plus the shooter, according to the RCMP.

The RCMP described the victims at the school as a 39-year-old educator, three girls aged 12, and two boys aged 12 and 13. The two killed at the house were a 39-year-old woman and an 11-year-old boy; McDonald identified them as the shooter's mother and her brother or stepbrother. Global News named the mother as Jennifer Jacobs and described the boy as the shooter's half-brother.

The minors who died were named by the RCMP, according to a report that CJDC-TV based on the lawsuits. They were Kylie Smith, Zoey Benoit and Ticaria Lampert, all 12; Abel Mwansa Jr., 12; and Ezekiel Schofield, 13. The educator was Shannda Aviugana-Durand, an education assistant. The same report named a 12-year-old survivor, Maya Gebala.

The lawsuits give the families' accounts, which are allegations in court filings and not findings. Aviugana-Durand's husband, Mark Stacey, said she was shot in front of her students and had been trying to stop the shooter; her own daughter, the suit says, saw it. Kylie Smith's guardians said a teacher and students tried for about forty-five minutes to save her. Abel Mwansa's parents said wounds to his hand, leg and chest left him bleeding for about forty-five minutes, and that his last words were "Tell my parents that I love them so much." Maya Gebala's suit says she was shot three times, that a classmate dragged her under a table, and that she has catastrophic brain injuries.
content.h2: What police said about the shooter
content.p: The RCMP named the shooter on 11 February as Jesse Van Rootselaar, an 18-year-old resident of Tumbler Ridge. McDonald said she had dropped out of the secondary school about four years earlier and was not a student there at the time. She was not related to any of the victims at the school, though Global News reported that her mother was a friend of the mother of Maya Gebala.

McDonald said police had attended the family home on multiple occasions over several years over concerns about her mental health, and that she had been apprehended at least twice under British Columbia's Mental Health Act and sometimes taken to hospital. He said that about two years earlier officers seized firearms from the house under the Criminal Code and that the lawful owner then petitioned for their return and got them back. She held a firearms licence that had expired in 2024 and had no weapons registered in her name, he said. McDonald also said that she was born male, had begun transitioning about six years earlier, and was publicly known as a woman. Police did not have a motive, McDonald said at the time. They found no note, according to Global News, and on 11 February the RCMP said it believed she acted alone, with no other outstanding suspects.

The RCMP said the shooter did not appear to have a target. "This suspect, for lack of a better word, hunting," McDonald said on 13 February, adding that she was "engaging with anyone they came in contact with." Video of the final moments inside the school showed a last burst of gunfire that was not aimed at anyone before she shot herself, he said; the video has not been released.

The question that has dominated the police work is where the weapons came from. Officers recovered a long gun and a modified handgun at the school, a description the RCMP later amended to a modified rifle, and two firearms at the house, McDonald said. The shotgun believed to have been used on the two victims at the home had never been seized by police. The main firearm used at the school had also never been seized, and its origin was "currently unknown", McDonald said on 13 February. He said investigators were looking at whether others had been involved in obtaining it.

By the end of that week the RCMP had interviewed more than 80 students, educators and first responders and was gathering video from phones, CCTV and officers' body cameras. It opened an online portal for the public to submit video from inside the school and asked people to be careful about sharing images online, saying that many circulating photos and videos wrongly claimed to show the suspect.

On 22 April Premier David Eby said RCMP had told the province the investigation was in its final stages, though without a timeline. Around the time the inquest was announced in March, an RCMP spokesperson from E Division said the investigation remained active and ongoing, and Eby told the legislature that the timetable depended on the police investigation, which he understood was examining the origin of the guns.
content.h2: The coroner's inquest and the inquiry debate
content.p: About three weeks after the killings, the BC chief coroner, Dr. Jatinder Baidwan, directed an inquest under Section 18 of the Coroners Act. He said an inquest would "publicly examine the circumstances surrounding the deaths", assess systemic and procedural issues, and make recommendations aimed at preventing similar losses. A jury of five to seven people will hear the evidence. He said it would examine how mental health and public safety systems intersect, how the shooter obtained guns, how people in crisis are identified and supported, and how northern and rural communities reach mental health care.

JURIST reported that the inquest would also look at the role of artificial intelligence, since one of the shooter's ChatGPT accounts had reportedly been banned but not reported to police, and the shooter had apparently created a second. The coroner said the investigation would "take as long as it takes" and that the inquest would not wait in the province's backlog; it would be scheduled once the information was available. At the announcement the venue had not been decided, and the date depended on the end of the coroner's investigation.

Opposition politicians called for more. Claire Rattee, the opposition critic for mental health and addictions, said a public inquiry could assign blame and look at systems in a way that an inquest, described as fact-finding and not fault-finding, could not. Eby said the inquest would be valuable but that the government would use all available tools to answer outstanding questions, and the public safety minister, Nina Krieger, said a joint federal and provincial commission was a possibility without committing to one.
content.h2: The ChatGPT account and the lawsuits
content.p: OpenAI has acknowledged that in June 2025, eight months before the shooting, it closed Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account because an automated system had picked up a breach of its usage policy and that it did not contact authorities. In a letter to Canada's artificial intelligence minister in February, Ann M. O'Leary, its vice president of global policy, wrote that the company "did not identify credible and imminent planning that met our threshold to refer the matter to law enforcement."

Seven lawsuits filed in April by victims' families name OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, and accuse its chatbot of "aiding and abetting a mass shooting," in the words of the CJDC-TV report. They were filed in California. The Boston Globe reported that the suits rely on a Wall Street Journal report that some OpenAI employees urged the company to contact the RCMP and that the company's leaders overruled its internal safety team. Those allegations are claims in court filings and have not been tested. In April, Altman published an open letter to the community. "I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement to the account that was banned in June," he wrote.

In the first days of September, 30 further suits were filed in US District Court in San Francisco by educators, a principal and students from the school, according to the Boston Globe. Eby said the plaintiffs had the province's full support and that the province intended to join the litigation as long as that did not interfere with the families' access to justice, and he said the new suits followed OpenAI walking away from a mediation process. OpenAI's chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, said the company was approaching the litigation "with respect for both the legal process and the families and victims" and would "continue to engage in good faith."

On 6 October 2026, according to the Canadian Press, a 30-year-old from Bellingham, Washington, James Cody Bryant, was arrested and charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country. The US Department of Justice alleges that he helped Van Rootselaar with plans to livestream the attack and helped her review her plans. A criminal complaint from the FBI, as described by the Canadian Press, alleges that he provided money and planning support in the months before the shooting. US authorities said the two met on a chat site that no longer exists and stayed in contact on Discord, which reported the conversations to authorities shortly after the shooting.

Bryant made a first court appearance in Seattle on the day of his arrest, and a detention hearing was scheduled for 13 October. He is to be held in custody until then. The CP24 report mentions no plea, and the allegations have not been tested in court. Acting US Attorney Neil Floyd said authorities had no information indicating that the two shared a political ideology or belonged to any organization. B.C. RCMP Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain said the Canadian investigation remained active and was looking at other individuals, but stopped short of promising further arrests.

The same report said survivors, victims' families and the B.C. government have all sued OpenAI in California, and that OpenAI is asking for many of the cases to be thrown out, contending that courts in British Columbia would be better placed to hear them.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called off a trip to Halifax and the Munich Security Conference, declared national mourning and ordered flags at government buildings to half-staff for seven days. Mayor Darryl Krakowka said he had lived in the town for 18 years and probably knew every one of the victims. In April he told reporters that grieving was happening unevenly: "Some have started grieving … and some others haven't."

The school district closed the town's schools for the rest of the week of the shooting. The attack revived the familiar Canadian argument over firearms. Global News noted that mass shootings in Canada, including the 1989 killing of 14 women at Montreal's École Polytechnique and the 2020 Nova Scotia rampage, have spurred changes to gun laws over the decades, and that the federal government was in the middle of a broad review of how firearms are classified.
